content:
Miles Thornton: Kicking off a quick architecture thread before we lock ADR language. Big question: centralized trigger evaluation service vs distributed per-component triggers (router, dns/edge, capacity, etc). We need something that won’t be flappy and we can audit later. 

Miles Thornton: Draft ADR doc (WIP): https://confluence.redwoodinference.com/display/ARCH/adr-0247-failover-trigger-engine-and-safety-guards

Jordan Lee: +1 we should settle this. Current state is basically “every system has its own heuristics” and it’s impossible to answer “why did we fail over” after the fact.

Mina Haddad: From Smart Routing side: distributed triggers scare me because each component sees partial truth and we end up with conflicting actions (routing policy flips while DNS stays put, etc). Also, rollback gets weird.

Ravi Menon: The counterpoint: centralized trigger service becomes a single point of failure + introduces coupling. If it’s down, do we just never fail over even if region is on fire?

Ethan Park: If the trigger engine is in control plane, it can be HA and region-independent (or at least multi-region). But yes, we need explicit degraded behavior if the trigger engine is unavailable.

Peter Holtz: I’m mostly worried about "distributed" becoming "we accidentally built 4 different state machines". That’s how we get flapping + midnight pages.

Aisha Bello: + audit + SLO alignment. To do error budget burn based automation, we need a single place that can evaluate multi-window/multi-burn and apply hysteresis consistently.

Zachary Hill: Another angle: safety checks (“safe-to-failover”) need to be enforced uniformly. If distributed, someone will skip a check in the name of "speed".

Victor Alvarez: For DNS/edge: I’m okay being an *actuator* but I don’t want edge itself making the call. Edge health checks are noisy and tend to false-positive under partial packet loss. Centralized evaluator can combine probes + 5xx + tail latency + saturation and decide.

Ravi Menon: What about latency to react? Distributed triggers could act fast (local threshold), centralized needs to ingest signals -> evaluate -> orchestrate.

Jordan Lee: Reaction time is mostly bounded by windowing/hysteresis anyway. If we’re using 2–5 min windows + hold-downs to avoid flaps, the extra few seconds of central eval isn’t the limiter.

Mina Haddad: Also progressive failover (5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100%) is inherently orchestrated. Hard to do that “distributed” without shared state.

Miles Thornton: Agree. I think we’re converging on centralized *trigger evaluation + state machine* with distributed *signal generation*. Components publish signals; evaluator decides.

Allison Grant: Observability benefit: one event stream for “entered degraded”, “initiated canary failover”, “rollback”, etc. If decisions are distributed, dashboards become a forensic nightmare.

Sean Gallagher: Jumping in. In the incidents review, the biggest gaps were: late detection + manual steps + debates about whether a signal is real. Centralized engine lets us encode the policy we keep debating, and we can tune it with postmortems.

Sean Gallagher: But I’m sympathetic to Ravi’s point: we need a plan if central engine is unreachable. I’d rather default to “don’t automatically flip traffic” than have edge do something unreviewed.

Ravi Menon: So: central engine is authoritative for *automatic* failover. If engine is down, we allow manual override (on-call) and keep system in “monitor-only” mode.

Zachary Hill: Yes + guardrails: manual override still must run safety checks unless an explicit “break-glass” is used (and that’s logged loudly).

Ethan Park: Control plane can expose `POST /failover/override` with RBAC + reason required. We can gate break-glass behind higher permission group.

Victor Alvarez: Make sure ADR calls out TTL strategy + propagation realities. Even if evaluator decides fast, DNS doesn’t.

Miles Thornton: Noted. We can separate “internal routing policy” (fast) vs “DNS/edge routing” (slower) as two actuators. Central engine coordinates both.

Aisha Bello: If we do that, we should define what constitutes “failover complete” for alerting. E.g., internal routing flipped for canary slice + SLO stabilizes, vs waiting for DNS propagation.

Jordan Lee: Pasting a strawman policy shape (this would live centrally):

```yaml
policy:
  region: us-east-1
  signals:
    - name: api_5xx_rate
      window: 5m
      threshold: 1.5%
    - name: p99_latency
      window: 5m
      threshold: 1800ms
    - name: net_packet_loss
      window: 2m
      threshold: 2%
  evaluate:
    mode: majority  # 2 of 3
    enter_hysteresis: 2m
    exit_hysteresis: 10m
    hold_down: 30m
  actions:
    - type: degrade
      scope: tier:free
    - type: canary_failover
      percent: 5
    - type: progressive_failover
      steps: [25, 50, 100]
  safety_checks:
    - target_capacity_headroom >= 20%
    - target_dependency_health == ok
    - routing_policy_sanity == ok
```

Mina Haddad: +1 to YAML schema living centrally. But we should keep routing policy complexity out of the trigger engine itself. Trigger decides state + target; routing system applies it.

Peter Holtz: Yep. Trigger engine shouldn’t become "routing policy 2.0".

Allison Grant: For metrics/events: please add explicit fields for decision inputs (signal values) and decision outputs (state transitions). That’s what we’ll need to explain behavior to enterprise.

Sean Gallagher: (reactions: :thumbsup: x4)

Ravi Menon: One more question: do we need per-component triggers at all, like local circuit breakers?

Ethan Park: We still want local protection mechanisms (timeouts, queue caps, load shedding) but those are “graceful degradation” controls, not “fail over to another region” triggers.

Aisha Bello: Exactly. Local circuit breakers are fine, but cross-region traffic shifting needs a single brain.

Victor Alvarez: + local mechanisms can be tuned without involving DNS. Keep them separate in docs so we don’t conflate.

Miles Thornton: Summary I’ll incorporate into ADR:
- Centralized trigger evaluation + state machine with auditable decisions
- Distributed signal generation (probes/metrics published into contract)
- Actuators: internal routing policy + DNS/edge changes orchestrated centrally
- If trigger engine unavailable: no automatic failover; manual override with RBAC + audit
- Local circuit breakers/load shedding remain distributed but do not initiate cross-region failover

Miles Thornton: Any objections before I update ADR text?

Mina Haddad: No objections. Please call out that progressive failover is required (not optional) for any automatic action.

Zachary Hill: Add explicit note: “manual override requires reason string + ticket link”. Also define break-glass logging.

Allison Grant: And add “decision log retention” requirement. At least 90d, ideally 180d for enterprise incident review.

Sean Gallagher: +1. Also, we should mention “monitor-only” stage in rollout (engine evaluates, emits recommendations, doesn’t act) so we can compare against what on-call did.

Jordan Lee: I’ll add a section in ADR on “monitor-only” mode + expected false positive/negative analysis.

Victor Alvarez: Please tag me when DNS section is updated; want to make sure we don’t promise instantaneous failover.

Miles Thornton: Will do. I’ll push ADR edits today and @mention here for final review.

--- next day ---

Miles Thornton: Updated ADR draft with the centralized vs distributed rationale + failure mode (“engine down => monitor-only + manual override”). Same link as above. Would love quick :eyes: esp from routing + control plane.

Ethan Park: Read it. Looks good. Minor: in the “single point of failure” section, call out that trigger service is deployed active/active across 2 control-plane regions and uses quorum storage for state.

Mina Haddad: Added comment in Confluence: clarify boundary between trigger engine and routing policy evaluation.

Aisha Bello: Commented on alerts: tie state transitions to burn-rate alerts so paging doesn’t double-fire.

Sean Gallagher: LGTM after those tweaks.

Miles Thornton: Awesome, thanks all. I’ll mark ADR as “Ready for approval” after I fold in comments.
